results.summary_before: This design simulates rolling a dice, displaying the result on a 7-segment display. Pulling input 0 high causes the dice to roll, and releasing it stops the roll. It requires an external 7-segment display connected to outputs 0-6 and a button connected to input 0. Silicon tests confirm it works, though the author notes that using the microswitch to stop the roll is a bit annoying.

results.summary_before: This design implements two pseudorandom number generators (PRNGs) using scan flip-flops and XOR gates, one with and one without a hardware trojan. It includes scan chain inputs for setting the PRNG state and an external trigger for the trojan, with outputs for both PRNGs and test points for inverters. Testing involves providing a clock, setting the scan inputs, toggling scan enable, and using a pattern generator and logic analyzer. The project is notable for demonstrating a hardware trojan in a PRNG context.

results.summary_before: This project is a simple 1-bit comparator that compares two input bits and indicates whether they are equal or which one is greater. It has two inputs (A and B) and three outputs: one for equality, one for A greater than B, and one for B greater than A. The design is purely combinational and can be tested by applying all four input combinations and observing the outputs, with LEDs recommended for visual indication. It is a basic educational logic circuit with no external hardware required beyond input switches and output LEDs.

results.summary_before: This project attempts to recreate the decoding logic of the vintage HP 5082-7500 display, a custom ASIC from the 1970s, on modern silicon. The design is incomplete and currently does not work, as indicated by the title. It would require a 4-bit BCD input and an LED dot-matrix display for testing, but no functional behavior is documented. The project is notable only as an unfinished attempt to reproduce historical logic.
